pages.text: Rain still glistened on the trunk road outside the school. At the zebra crossing, Eyram raised her red STOP sign and kept her classmates well back on the pavement. A trotro came towards them, overloaded and far too fast. The driver braked hard. The worn tyres slid on the wet tar, and the minibus skidded right past the white stripes before it shuddered to a stop. Nobody was hurt, because the students had waited until the wheels stopped turning. Kojo stared at a smooth, bald rear tyre. “Why could the brakes not stop it on the line?”

pages.alt: Standing well back on a raised school pavement in light rain, Eyram holds a red STOP sign keeping younger pupils safe while a heavily loaded minibus skids across wet white zebra stripes.

pages.text: In Integrated Science, the teacher turned the near-miss into an investigation. Kojo hooked a spring balance to a loaded wooden block and pulled it across three surfaces: dry sandpaper, dry wood, and smooth wet plastic. On the wet plastic, the reading fell sharply. There was far less friction. “Brakes do not work by magic,” the teacher said. “Brake fluid carries pressure to the brakes. They slow the wheels and turn the vehicle’s kinetic energy—its movement energy—into heat. But the tyres must still grip the road. The grooves in a tyre push water out of the way. A worn tyre cannot do that, so on a wet road it slides.”

pages.text: “Why does overloading matter?” Eyram asked. The teacher wrote on the board. “First, more mass moving at the same speed means more momentum and more kinetic energy. So an overloaded vehicle needs a longer distance to stop. Second, heavy goods piled on the roof rack raise the centre of gravity, and the bus can topple on a bend. Third, think about pressure. Pressure is force divided by area: P = F ÷ A. It is measured in pascals, or newtons per square metre. A wide seatbelt spreads the stopping force over a large area of the chest and hips, so the pressure on the body is low. A thin rope would cut in.”

pages.text: On Wednesday, Corporal Adjei of the police Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD) spoke at a Social Studies road-safety forum. “Do not call road crashes ‘accidents’ that nobody could prevent,” he said. “Most begin with a choice: speeding through town, overtaking on a bend or a hill, driving tired or drunk, ignoring seatbelts and crash helmets, or running on worn tyres. Every crash drains hospital blood banks. It can leave children without parents and families without a breadwinner. And it costs Ghana millions of cedis in repairs and emergency care.”

pages.text: In RME, Abdulai shared a talk he had with his uncle, a trotro driver, at the lorry station. “My uncle says every passenger is somebody’s whole world,” Abdulai told the class. “In Islam, protecting life is a duty, called hifz al-nafs. A driver who uses bald tyres or overtakes carelessly breaks that duty. Christians are commanded not to take life and to love their neighbour, and that applies behind a steering wheel too. And our elders teach boasetɔ, patience. It is far better to arrive ten minutes late than never to arrive at all.”

pages.text: The school did not stop at talk. Together with the Parent-Teacher Association, the municipal roads engineer, and Corporal Adjei, it petitioned the assembly. Soon there were speed humps, rumble strips, and clear warning signs near the school gate. Eyram’s road wardens also taught the primary pupils the crossing rule. Stop at the kerb. Look left, look right, and look left again. Make sure drivers have seen you. Obey the crossing guard. Cross only when traffic has stopped in every lane—above all on wet tar, where physics never bends for impatient feet.

activities.question: Why did the minibus with worn tyres skid past the crossing even though the driver braked?
options: Rainwater increased friction ten times so the wheels spun faster forward
Water reduced friction between smooth tyres and the road, causing skidding
Pressing hydraulic brakes destroys gravity underneath a moving minibus

activities.question: Using Pressure = Force ÷ Area, why is a wide flat seatbelt safer than a thin cord during sudden braking?
options: A larger area spreads the stopping force, so the pressure on the body is lower
A wide seatbelt increases pressure so sharply that it cuts through clothing
Increasing surface area multiplies total force by a thousand

activities.question: How does stacking heavy cargo high on a vehicle’s roof rack affect its stability on a sharp bend?
options: It removes all mass and momentum from the moving vehicle
It lowers the centre of gravity beneath the road surface
It raises vehicle centre of gravity, making it unstable and prone to overturn

activities.question: Apply it: You are waiting at a zebra crossing during rain. What is the safest action?
options: Step out as soon as a driver waves, without checking the other lane
Wait on the pavement, check both ways, and cross only when traffic stops
Run across because wet roads help cars stop faster

activities.prompt: Put the steps for crossing a road safely in the correct order.
items: Stand back from the kerb, observing vehicle speeds and wet road conditions.
Look left, right, and left again, watching drivers before stepping out.
Cross only when vehicles have stopped or all lanes are completely clear.
Walk briskly straight across, still watching the traffic.

activities.definition: A force that opposes motion between two surfaces that are touching.
distractors: A non-contact magnetic force pulling iron filings through empty space
The upward buoyant push of water on a floating canoe

glossary.definition: The force opposing motion between two surfaces in contact; grooved tyre treads preserve friction on wet roads.
The product of a vehicle mass and velocity, determining the force required to bring it to a stop.
The perpendicular force acting per unit area of a surface (P = F ÷ A), measured in pascals (Pa) or newtons per square metre (N/m²).
The single point through which the entire weight of a body appears to act; keeping it low and over a wide base increases stability.
An Akan virtue meaning patience, restraint, and calm self-mastery—vital for safe driving and peaceful civic life.
